entries.title: Francisco Goya: When Reason Sleeps and Monsters Emerge
entries.body_text: Francisco Goya was born on March 30, 1746, in Fuendetodos, Spain. Court painter to the Spanish Crown, he was also its most unflinching critic. A mysterious illness left him profoundly deaf around 1793, and the isolation that followed pushed his work toward the psychological and the grotesque. In 1799 he published 'Los Caprichos,' a series of 80 satirical etchings and aquatints skewering the superstitions, hypocrisies, and cruelties of Spanish society. Plate 43 — 'El sueño de la razón produce monstruos' (The Sleep of Reason Produces Monsters) — depicts a man slumped at his desk while owls and bats swarm around him, a warning that the abandonment of rational thought breeds darkness. Two decades later, between 1819 and 1823, Goya painted directly onto the plaster walls of his home, the 'Quinta del Sordo,' producing the fourteen murals now known as the Black Paintings. 'Saturn Devouring His Son' — a wild-eyed giant cramming a small human body into his mouth — is the most viscerally disturbing image in the Western canon. Transferred to canvas and now housed in the Museo del Prado, the Black Paintings remain one of art history's most astonishing acts of private, uncompromising darkness.

entries.title: Henry Fuseli's 'The Nightmare': Gothic Horror Before Gothic Horror Existed
entries.body_text: When Henry Fuseli first exhibited 'The Nightmare' at the Royal Academy Summer Exhibition of 1782, it transfixed London. The canvas shows a woman in white collapsed across a bed in deep, helpless sleep, a leering incubus crouched on her chest, and a wild-eyed horse — the 'nightmare mare' of Germanic and Norse folklore — thrusting its head through heavy dark curtains. Fuseli had taken the folk terror of sleep paralysis — the crushing sensation of a demonic presence holding the dreamer immobile — and made it monumental, sensational, and strangely erotic. Born Johann Heinrich Füssli on February 7, 1741, in Zurich, Fuseli trained in theology before moving to London and remaking himself as a painter of the extreme and the visionary. He later became a professor and Keeper at the Royal Academy, where he lectured on Shakespeare and Homer. But it is 'The Nightmare' — reproduced in engravings sold across Europe, inspiring Erasmus Darwin's poetry and a satirical print lampooning Prime Minister Pitt — that secured his place in art history as the father of Gothic visual horror.

entries.title: Leonora Carrington on Rebellion and the Work of Becoming an Artist
entries.body_text: I didn't have time to be anyone's muse. I was too busy rebelling against my family and learning to be an artist.

entries.title: William Blake on Perception, Infinity, and the Doors That Limit Us
entries.body_text: If the doors of perception were cleansed every thing would appear to man as it is, Infinite. For man has closed himself up, till he sees all things thro' narrow chinks of his cavern.

entries.source_name: Blake, William. 'The Marriage of Heaven and Hell.' Illuminated book, c. 1790-93. Plate 14, 'A Memorable Fancy.' William Blake Archive (blakearchive.org).
entries.rights_note: Public domain. William Blake died August 12, 1827; 'The Ancient of Days' created 1794. Image sourced from Wikimedia Commons.

entries.title: Odilon Redon on Making the Invisible Visible
entries.body_text: My whole originality, therefore, consists in making imaginary beings live, according to the laws of probability, by putting, as much as possible, the logic of the visible at the service of the invisible.

entries.rights_note: Public domain. Odilon Redon died July 6, 1916; 'The Cyclops' created c. 1914. Image sourced from Wikimedia Commons.

entries.title: Katsushika Hokusai: Born on Halloween, Painter of Ghosts
entries.body_text: Katsushika Hokusai was born on October 31, 1760, in the Honjo district of Edo (present-day Tokyo) — a date that feels less like coincidence and more like destiny for an artist who produced some of the most unsettling ghost imagery in Japanese printmaking history. While Western audiences know him primarily for 'The Great Wave off Kanagawa' (c. 1831), Hokusai also produced the 'Hyaku Monogatari' (One Hundred Ghost Stories, 1831-32), a series of woodblock prints depicting traditional Japanese yūrei (ghosts) and supernatural beings drawn from the 'kaidan' storytelling tradition. Among the most chilling is 'Kohada Koheiji,' in which the murdered kabuki actor Koheiji returns as a decomposing, grinning spectre rising through a screen of lotus leaves to haunt his killer. Hokusai changed his name more than thirty times throughout his life. In his final years he called himself Gakyo Rojin Manji — 'Old Man Mad About Painting.' He died on May 10, 1849, at 88, reportedly saying: 'If only Heaven will give me just another ten years — just five more years — I could become a real painter.'
